content: The term peptic is an adjective used to describe any part of the body that typically contains an acidic lumen. It is a term commonly employed in medical and veterinary contexts, particularly in reference to human anatomy. Under normal circumstances, the peptic regions of the human body include the stomach and the duodenum. In individuals with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), the esophagus—especially its lower portion—may also become acidic. Additionally, individuals with a Meckel's diverticulum may have cells within the diverticulum that produce acid, predisposing them to peptic ulcers and potential perforation. In cases of altered anatomy, such as after a gastrectomy or an esophagectomy with ileal transplantation to replace the esophagus, acidity may occur in regions of the body that are not typically acidic. However, in normal human anatomy and in the vast majority of individuals, the gastrointestinal tract is the only part of the body considered peptic. A common issue associated with peptic regions is the development of peptic ulcers. These ulcers are most frequently caused by bacterial infections, rather than the acidic environment itself.
